A video documenting the Q&A session from one of Apple's most significant events over the past 20 years is being widely circulated online—go watch it before it gets taken down. Here is the clip.

Watch it now before Apple removes the video

Even if you weren't closely following Apple news back then, you've probably heard of the 'Antennagate' scandal, and the impromptu press conference that forced Jobs to cut short his family vacation in Hawaii to attend.

If you only started following us after the incident, here's a recap: shortly after the iPhone 4 went on sale, users discovered that holding the phone in a certain way could cause the cellular signal to drop dramatically.

The controversy blew up so badly that Apple was forced to hold an emergency event just a few weeks after the iPhone 4 launched.

At the event, Jobs explained that signal attenuation wasn't unique to the iPhone 4, and offered users two options: a free bumper case to prevent their hands from directly touching the antenna, or a full refund.

After the event, Jobs sat down for a Q&A session with then–Chief Operating Officer Tim Cook and Apple's Senior Vice President of Mac Hardware Engineering, Bob Mansfield.

Since then, multiple accounts of that Q&A have circulated, including a recollection by John Gruber—who asked a question that year that got Jobs, Cook and Mansfield to pull unsheathed iPhones out of their pockets, producing one of the most unforgettable photos of that era. The actual video of the session, however, never surfaced—until now.

Earlier this week, the YouTube channel Sir Mix-A-Lot Rare Music (which, apparently, has nothing to do with the actual Sir Mix-A-Lot) uploaded the entire 47-minute Q&A session, which you can watch below:

There is currently no information on how the channel obtained the footage, nor whether Apple will file a copyright takedown request. But now that the video has leaked, even if the original is removed, copies will easily resurface elsewhere.

The fact that the video still hasn't been taken down is itself a good sign. Still, if you want to witness this piece of Apple history with your own eyes, you'd better watch it while you can.

Were you following Apple's 'Antennagate' back then? Let us know in the comments.
